title: Genesis 43:1–14
context: The famine bites again. Judah refuses a second trip without Benjamin, pledges himself as surety, and Israel yields: gifts, double money, the boy, and a prayer to God Almighty for mercy before the man—plus a bereaved father’s surrender.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Classic Arminian and Reformed comment on Genesis 43:1–14, in the writers’ own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Judah's conscience had lately smitten him for what he had done a great while ago against Joseph; and as an evidence of the truth of his repentance, he is ready to undertake, as far as a man could do it, for Benjamin's security. He will not only not wrong him but will do all he can to protect him. This is such restitution as the case will admit: when he knew not how he could retrieve Joseph, he would make some amends for the irreparable injury he had done him, by doubling his care concerning Benjamin.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 43:9)

reformed.quote: It may, however, here be asked, how Jacob could have supported his family, even for a few days, with so small a quantity of corn: for, suppose it to be granted that several asses were conducted by each of the brethren, what was this to sustain three hundred persons? For, since Abraham had a much larger number of servants, and mention has been made above of the servants of Isaac; it is incredible that Jacob was so entirely destitute, as to have no servants left.

verses.text: The famine was severe in the land.
verses.arminianNotes:
Severity, not a passing shortage. Canaan’s need pushes the stalled household back toward Egypt.

Hardship is authentic and morally weighty. Hunger will press choices; it does not erase them. The brothers must still decide how to go.
verses.reformedNotes:
The famine Joseph interpreted now presses Jacob’s tent. Severity is providence, not accident.

God uses empty jars to move the sons toward the brother they sold. The land’s pain serves the covenant’s path to Egypt.

verses.text: When they had eaten up the grain which they had brought out of Egypt, their father said to them, “Go again, buy us a little more food.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The first load is gone. Israel says go again, as if the man in Egypt had not named Benjamin. Need speaks; memory lags.

Arminians find a father’s responsible care and a delay. He still hopes to feed the house without sending the remaining son of Rachel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Empty sacks reopen the file. “A little more food” understates what the journey will cost.

The grain God stored in Egypt is meant to draw them down again. The father’s short request sits inside a longer decree.

verses.text: Judah spoke to him, saying, “The man solemnly warned us, saying, ‘You shall not see my face, unless your brother is with you.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Judah reports the solemn warning. No face, no grain—without Benjamin. He will not pretend the governor’s word was a suggestion.

Pastorally: truth-telling here is costly honesty. Judah names the condition rather than managing the father with a softer lie.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Solemnly warned” is legal weight. Joseph’s face is the gate of life for this family, and he has locked it to Benjamin’s presence.

The unnamed “man” is the brother they do not recognize. Providence speaks through a warning they must take at face value.

verses.text: If you’ll send our brother with us, we’ll go down and buy you food;
verses.arminianNotes:
If you send, we will go. Judah puts the decision in Israel’s hands without stealing it. Food is tied to a father’s yes.

Judah states the condition and offers obedience on those terms. They will not go as rebels; they wait for send-authority they can then own.
verses.reformedNotes:
The if-clause is household order. Judah will not freelance the heir of Rachel south.

God will get Benjamin to Egypt, and He will do it through this father’s reluctant sending, not around it.

verses.text: but if you don’t send him, we won’t go down, for the man said to us, ‘You shall not see my face, unless your brother is with you.’”
verses.arminianNotes:
The negative is as clear as the offer. Without Benjamin, the brothers will not go down. Repeating the man’s word keeps the family from a doomed trip.

Classical Arminians honor this as responsible refusal. Going without Benjamin would be theater, not faith.
verses.reformedNotes:
Refusal to go is obedience to the governor’s oath, not mutiny against Jacob.

The door Joseph shut is the door God is using. The brothers cannot work around the test.

verses.text: Israel said, “Why did you treat me so badly, telling the man that you had another brother?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Pain speaks as blame. Israel hears the disclosure as harm done to him. Grief still names Joseph “no more” in the background.

Wounded parents can accuse the messengers of providence. The question is unfair and human; grace will yet hold this house together.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Treat me so badly” locates the wound in the father’s chest. He cannot yet see that telling the truth was the only path to Simeon and to bread.

God is not the accused, but He is not absent. The badly-felt disclosure is how the dreams of chapter 37 keep coming true.

verses.text: They said, “The man asked directly concerning ourselves, and concerning our relatives, saying, ‘Is your father still alive? Have you another brother?’ We just answered his questions. Is there any way we could know that he would say, ‘Bring your brother down’?”
verses.arminianNotes:
They answer: we were questioned; we told the truth; we could not foresee the demand. Agency and ignorance sit together.

Honest speech can still open a door you did not choose. They remain responsible for truth-telling, not for the governor’s next move.
verses.reformedNotes:
Careful questions from Joseph pull the family map into the open. They could not know—and God did.

The unrecognized brother scripts the interrogation. Providence uses ordinary Q-and-A to fetch Benjamin without the brothers grasping why.

verses.text: Judah said to Israel, his father, “Send the boy with me, and we’ll get up and go, so that we may live, and not die, both we, and you, and also our little ones.
verses.arminianNotes:
Judah takes the lead Reuben failed. Send the boy with me—that we may live, including little ones. The plea is for the whole house, not for Judah’s honor.

Arminian readers hear a grace-enabled turn: the brother who once sold Joseph now stakes life on bringing Rachel’s other son home.
verses.reformedNotes:
Judah, not Reuben, becomes the speaker of life-and-death. “Little ones” widens the stake to the next generation of promise.

The lion-line begins to look like a pledge rather than a seller of brothers. God is reshaping Judah under famine.

verses.text: I’ll be collateral for him. From my hand will you require him. If I don’t bring him to you, and set him before you, then let me bear the blame forever;
verses.arminianNotes:
Surety language: from my hand, blame forever. Judah offers himself in Benjamin’s place if the boy is lost. This is not cheap talk; chapter 44 will spend it.

Substitution offered is a moral act. Grace can turn a guilty man into a pledge. He must still keep the word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Pledge, require, blame forever: Judah becomes surety. The future king-tribe learns substitution under pressure.

This vow foreshadows a greater Brother who will not fail the Father’s charge. Here it is still a man’s oath; God will use it to break Joseph’s test.
verses.keyContrast: Both honor Judah’s surety as a turn from chapter 37. Arminians underline a responsible, grace-enabled pledge he must keep; Reformed commentators typically underline God’s reshaping of Judah toward substitution that serves the larger preservation of the seed.

verses.text: for if we hadn’t delayed, surely we would have returned a second time by now.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Delay has a cost: two trips lost. Judah names the father’s hesitation without sneering.

In practice: waiting in fear is still a choice with consequences. Mercy remains; the calendar of hunger does not.
verses.reformedNotes:
Twice-returned is the road not taken. Delay was Jacob’s, and it has lengthened Simeon’s custody.

Even wasted time sits inside the famine God timed. The second trip will still land on Joseph’s noon meal.

verses.text: Their father, Israel, said to them, “If it must be so, then do this: Take from the choice fruits of the land in your bags, and carry down a present for the man, a little balm, a little honey, spices and myrrh, nuts, and almonds;
verses.arminianNotes:
If it must be so: Israel yields. Gifts from a starving land—balm, honey, gum, myrrh, nuts—are the old Jacob, still trying to soften a face with presents.

Yielding is not unbelief’s opposite. He sends what he can. The present is a father’s responsible attempt, not a bribe that replaces prayer (v. 14).
verses.reformedNotes:
Israel, the covenant name, now speaks. The present is thin luxury from a famine country—dignity offered to an unknown lord.

God lets Jacob be Jacob, gifts and all, while the true provision is already stored in Egypt. The man will not be bought; he will weep.

verses.text: and take double money in your hand, and take back the money that was returned in the mouth of your sacks. Perhaps it was an oversight.
verses.arminianNotes:
Double money, and the returned silver carried back. “Perhaps it was an oversight” is honesty hoping for a clean ledger.

Classical Arminians honor the restitution. They will not keep what landed in the sacks. Integrity is a grace-enabled duty even when they did not steal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Oversight is Jacob’s best guess. The reader knows Joseph ordered the money back.

They return silver God used to frighten them (42:28). Providence can hide a gift inside what feels like a trap.

verses.text: Take your brother also, get up, and return to the man.
verses.arminianNotes:
Take also your brother. The sentence Israel would not speak in 42:38 now comes out. Jacob finally tells them to go again.

Hard obedience can be late and still genuine. Sending Benjamin is trust under protest, not enthusiasm—and it is still a yes.
verses.reformedNotes:
The boy is released by the father’s mouth. Go again to the man aims them at Joseph unawares.

The heir of Rachel moves toward Egypt because Israel finally speaks the word God has been waiting to use.

verses.text: May God Almighty give you mercy before the man, that he may release to you your other brother and Benjamin. If I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved.”
verses.arminianNotes:
El Shaddai is named: grant mercy before the man; send back Simeon and Benjamin. Then the wounded surrender—“if I am bereaved, I am bereaved.” Prayer and lament share a verse.

Wesleyan Arminians see a petition. Mercy is asked because mercy can be granted. Israel does not fatalize God; he asks, then yields the children he cannot keep by clutching.
verses.reformedNotes:
God Almighty—the name of chapter 17—is invoked over an Egyptian doorway. Mercy before “the man” is the right request; the man is already Joseph.

The bereaved clause is not unbelief’s last word but a saint’s emptying. God will answer beyond the prayer: not only two brothers, but Joseph himself.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear El Shaddai asked for mercy. Arminians emphasize a sincere petition that may be granted or refused; Reformed commentators typically emphasize that the Almighty already has the mercy in hand, including the unrecognized brother who will show it.
